newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Lingering German rate cut hopes fade on M3.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Lingering German rate cut hopes fade on M3.

text.p: Lingering hopes for another easing in German interest rates receded further on Thursday after news of a slight pick-up in M3 money supply growth and in business confidence in August.

Meanwhile, as expected, the Bundesbank held its three key interest rates steady at its regular fortnightly meeting, setting its main money market rate, or repo, at an unchanged three percent for the next three weeks.
M3, which the Bundesbank sees as its most important indicator of inflationary trends, grew at an annualised rate of 8.7 percent, compared with 8.6 percent in July.

The figure was well above analysts' forecasts of about eight percent and marked the first acceleration in M3 growth since February. The Bundesbank said the rise was partly explained by buoyant bank lending, a sign of increasing economic activity.
Economists said the data suggested there was no need for another credit easing in the current economic cycle but stressed that any monetary tightening remained far off.

Remarks by certain Bundesbank officials in recent weeks had fuelled market talk that another repo rate cut was on the cards this year, even though the Bundesbank cut the rate by 30 basis points to three percent, an historic low, in late August.

"I think this M3 number has reduced the chance of another rate cut," said Armin Kayser, an economist at SBC in Frankfurt. "The Bundesbank cannot be sure that M3 will reach its target corridor this year."

Separately, the Munich-based Ifo economic research institute reported a modest rise in its business climate index for August to 94.4 from a revised 94.0 in July. That was broadly was in line with analysts' forecasts.

Joachim Fels, senior Germany economist at Morgan Stanley in London, said, "The Bundesbank has done a lot to stimulate the economy in the last 12 to 15 months and now the effect of its monetary loosening is being shown in economic activity and business sentiment. At the same time there is no need for rates to rise."
The M3 news initially pushed German bond prices lower, but the losses were slight and bonds were supported by the Ifo index, which had recently been rumoured to be as high as 96.
The yield on the benchmark 10-year, 6.25 percent government bond was quoted at 6.18 percent at 1130 GMT, up from 6.16 in early trade before the data.

Neither M3 nor the Ifo index clashed with forecasts that German economic growth and inflation would remain tame for the foreseeable future despite a return to strong growth of 1.5 percent in the second quarter, economists said.
Consumer spending was harnessed by low wage increases, the fear of unemployment and planned cuts in welfare spending while corporate investment remained stagnant, they said.

The Bundesbank said M3, which comprises cash in circulation as well as time, sight and short-term savings deposits, was buoyed by growth in bank lending which expanded at an annualised rate of seven percent over the last seven months.
Meanwhile money capital formation -- the process of taking money out of bank desposits and investing it in bonds -- weakened, thereby contributing to the M3 gains.
But economists said the long-term trend continued to show a slowdown in M3 growth and noted that the six-month annualised growth fell to 6.8 percent in August from 8.6 percent in July.
